newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Canberra's lawyers doubt mine lease validity.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Canberra's lawyers doubt mine lease validity.

text.p: A new High Court decision on Aborigines' native title may invalidate mining leases granted since 1994, lawyers have told the Australian government.

Pastoralists may no longer have a free reign on how they use their land and it may become harder for them to get variations on their land leases, the lawyers have told the government. The legal opinions were released by the government on Thursday.
The legal implications arise from the High Court's December extension of Aborigines' native land title -- which it invented in 1992 -- to land that had been leased to pastoralists.
The federal government responded to the invention of native title -- in the Mabo case -- by regulating it in 1993 in the Native Title Act (NTA).
For example, the act gave aborigines a right to negotiate over what happened to land they had an interest in.

But since the Act became law at the beginning of 1994 it has been but assumed that pastoral leases are unaffected and that native title existed only on land that the Crown still controlled. In December the court ruled otherwise.

"Acts done since 1 January 1994 in relation to pastoral lease land which did not comply with the NTA may turn out to be invalid -- eg, the grant of mining titles over pastoral lease land without following the right-to-negotiate procedure," the govewrnment's lawyers said in their assessment of the new case.

"The NTA may also restrict the variation of pastoral lease conditions or the grant of additional permits required by the pastoralist before engaging in non-pastoral activiites on the leased land," they said.
The court ruling had made it clear pastoralists' leases were valid, and that their rights would prevail over the Aborigines'.
Miners and farmers have demanded government action to resolve the uncertainty that now affects their businesses and the federal and state governments met on Wednesday to discuss the issue.
"However, there may be uncertainty in particular cases as to the extent of a pastoralist's rights ..." the lawyers said.

The new ruling -- the Wik case, named after the Wik Aboriginal people -- has revived the vexing question of Aboriginal land entitlements, which Australia thought it had finally resolved in the 1993 negotiations over the original case.
